market_context: United States/general English; home spoilage signs in fresh fish and fillets
title: How to tell if fish has gone bad

seo.title: How to tell if fish is bad: smell, texture and appearance
seo.meta_description: Fresh fish should smell mild, not sour, rancid or ammonia-like. Soft flesh, drying edges and strong odor are signs of poor freshness or spoilage.
seo.search_intent: Identify useful spoilage signs in fresh fish and know when to discard it.

excerpt: Smell is one of the most useful signs: FDA says fresh fish should smell mild and fresh, not strongly fishy, sour, rancid or ammonia-like. Flesh should be firm and spring back when pressed. In fillets, darkening, discoloration or drying around the edges indicate loss of freshness, although no home test replaces correct cold storage.
content_html:
Fish spoils quickly and there is no single perfect home test. The best judgment combines smell, texture, appearance and storage time. One unusual sign can be ambiguous; several abnormal signs together are a clear reason to discard the fish.

Fresh fish should smell mild

FDA says fresh fish should smell fresh and mild, not strongly fishy, sour or ammonia-like. Spoiled seafood can develop sour, rancid, fishy or ammonia odors, and those smells often become stronger during cooking.

If raw or cooked seafood smells sour, rancid or strongly fishy, FDA advises not eating it. Ammonia odor in cooked seafood is also a discard sign.

The flesh should be firm

Fresh whole fish should have firm flesh. Fresh fillets should also feel firm and spring back after gentle pressure. Extremely soft, mushy or slimy texture is more concerning.

What to look for in whole fish

FDA buying guidance looks for clear, shiny eyes, firm flesh and red gills without an off odor. Appearance varies by species and treatment, so color by itself is not proof of freshness.

What to look for in fillets

Fresh fillets should be firm and should not show marked discoloration, darkening or drying around the edges. Previously frozen fish may not have every visual trait of never-frozen fish, but it should still smell mild rather than sour or rancid.

The clock matters even if it smells fine

Raw seafood is highly perishable. USDA recommends keeping raw fish and shellfish at 40°F (4°C) or below for only 1–2 days before cooking or freezing. A seemingly normal smell should not be used to stretch that window indefinitely.

Cooking does not rescue spoiled fish

Heat destroys many microorganisms, but it does not turn clearly deteriorated seafood into a reasonable food choice. FDA notes that spoilage odors can actually become stronger during cooking.

The practical takeaway

Discard fish with sour, rancid, ammonia-like or persistently unpleasant odor, especially when it is also soft, slimy or visibly abnormal. Even when it seems normal, respect the short 1–2 day refrigerator window for raw fish.

faq.question: What should fresh fish smell like?
faq.answer: Fresh and mild. FDA says it should not smell strongly fishy, sour, rancid or ammonia-like.

faq.question: Does soft fish mean it is spoiled?
faq.answer: Very soft, mushy or slimy texture is concerning, especially with bad odor or prolonged storage.

faq.question: How long does fresh fish keep in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: USDA recommends only 1–2 days at 40°F (4°C) or below before cooking or freezing.
